title: Calibration overlay and ruler: is the pixel scale right?
summary: An image with a feature of known size marked by two picked points, the resulting millimetres per pixel, and a scale bar. It checks the conversion from pixels to physical units before any measurement is trusted.

media.alt: A grey frame of a flame-like glow with a reference rectangle of 140 pixels labelled 10 mm, two picked end points, a scale label of 0.0714 mm per pixel and a white 5 mm scale bar.
media.caption: Reference render with synthetic demonstration data (design-system gallery).

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data.

read_the_figure.question: Is the pixel scale right?
read_the_figure.axes: x and y: pixel coordinates (y downward as in an image), 0 to 360 and 0 to 240. Grey levels: intensity. Amber rectangle: the reference object. Rose crosses: the two picked points. White bar: scale bar. Text: calibration result.
look_at: Are the two crosses on the true ends of the reference?
Does the quoted scale follow from the known size and the pixel distance?
Does the scale bar have the length it claims, in pixels?
Is the reference in the same plane as the object to be measured?
read_the_figure.proves: A reference of known size with its end points picked gives the scale, and a scale bar of the right length shows the reader the size of things. It does not prove the optics are free of distortion, nor that the reference lies in the focal plane.
if_wrong: Scale bar whose length does not match the quoted scale: in this render, see below.
Picks that are a few pixels off at both ends: a 2 pixel error on 140 pixels is 1.4 percent.
Reference at a different distance from the camera than the object: perspective changes the scale.

terms.meaning: Determining the factor that converts image pixels to physical length.
Known length divided by its length in pixels.
A point on the image chosen (by clicking or by a detector) to mark an end of the reference.
Line of fixed physical length drawn in the image; it carries the calibration to the reader.
Error that arises when objects are at different distances from the camera, so one scale does not fit all.

remember: A scale bar of length L_bar must be L_bar / s pixels long.
Two picks of error delta_p each give a relative error about sqrt(2) delta_p / N.
Calibrate in the plane of the measurement and re-check if the camera moves.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Position gives pixel coordinates, brightness gives light. The amber rectangle and double arrow mark the reference, the rose crosses show where the end points were picked, and the amber label states the known length. The black label at top left states the resulting scale, and the white bar at lower right is the scale bar with its length.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: A measurement from an image is a pixel count times a scale, so the scale is the single most important number. Drawing the reference, the picks and the result in one picture lets the reader check each step: are the picks on the ends, does the arithmetic work, and does the final bar look the right size next to the reference.

understand.title: Read this reference render
understand.text: Q1: What is the scale? The reference is 140 px wide (x = 60 to 200) and 10.0 mm long, so 10/140 = 0.0714 mm/px, as the label says. Q2: How long should a 5 mm scale bar be? 5/0.0714 = 70 px. Q3: Is the drawn bar right? It runs from x = 240 to 340, 100 px, which at this scale is 7.1 mm, not 5: the bar is wrong by 43 percent. A reader who trusts it would overestimate every length.

understand.title: The must-check list, explained
understand.text: Scale bar: the bar is the only part of the figure a reader will use to estimate lengths without arithmetic, so it must be computed from the calibration and checked. Here it is not.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: A scale is only as good as two clicks: with the reference spanning 140 px, a 2 px error at each end gives an error of about 2 percent. The scale bar must be checked against the scale: in this render the bar is labelled 5 mm and is 100 px long, but at 0.0714 mm/px 5 mm is 70 px, so the bar represents 7.1 mm. A calibration in one plane does not hold for objects nearer or farther, and lens distortion makes the scale vary across the image.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: A calibration grid or target with many points, which gives scale and distortion; a ruler placed in the scene and left in a reference frame; an automatic detection of the target corners with a stated uncertainty.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Add a second calibration at a different position in the image and show the two scales; draw the scale bar from the formula L_bar / s.

steps.title: Scale from a reference
steps.note: Pick the end points, count pixels along the line.

steps.title: Length of a scale bar and the pick error
steps.note: delta_p is the error of each pick in pixels.

worked.title: Check the scale bar and the pick error
worked.problem: A 10.0 mm reference spans 140 px. How long (px) must a 5 mm bar be? What is the relative error of the scale if each pick is uncertain by 2 px?
worked.answer: A 5 mm bar should be 70 px long (the render's 100 px bar shows 7.1 mm); each pick uncertain by 2 px gives a 2 percent uncertainty in the scale.

analyze.q: The camera moves by a few millimetres towards the object after calibration. What happens to every measurement?
Why use a calibration target with many points instead of one pair?

evaluate.q: Is a calibration photographed once at the start of a campaign enough?

create: Draw the bar from the formula and check it in code before the figure is saved.
Add a second reference at the top of the image and plot the scale against y.

checks.q: What does the scale bar do for a reader?
checks.answer: It carries the calibration into the picture so lengths can be read directly.

checks.q: A feature of 85 px, scale 0.0714 mm/px. Length?
The label says 0.0714 mm/px but the bar is 100 px for 5 mm (0.05 mm/px). What do you trust?
checks.hint: Which is derived from the reference?
checks.answer: The scale derived from the reference and picks (0.0714) is the measurement; the bar disagrees and must be redrawn.
